author: AfricanFeminism
title: Beyond Translation: Reimagining Feminist Funding for Portuguese-Speaking Africa
content:
“Portuguese-speaking Africa is not on the margins of Africa’s feminist movement. It is an essential part of it.”




Across Africa, feminist movements have long challenged systems of inequality, responded to crises, created new possibilities for minoritized and excluded communities. Philanthropy has been integral to advances toward just and equal African societies. Yet within the current global and continental landscape of feminist philanthropy, some communities and movements remain largely unseen. 




The Portuguese-speaking African countries that include Angola, Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Equatorial Guinea and São Tomé and Principe, represent diverse histories, political realities and social contexts. Their feminist movements are dynamic, innovative and deeply rooted in their communities. They are advancing gender justice in contexts shaped by economic deprivation and inequality, climate change, difficult democratic transitions, shrinking civic space and gender-based violence.




Despite this important work, these movements continue to face significant barriers to accessing resources, networks and spaces where Africa’s feminist priorities are shaped. The challenge is not a lack of organizing. It is a fragmented funding ecosystem that has not yet fully recognized or responded to the diversity of Africa’s feminist movements. 




The cost of being overlooked

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Para além da tradução: repensar o financiamento feminista na África lusófona
content:
“A África lusófona não está à margem do movimento feminista africano. É uma parte integrante dele.”




Em toda a África, os movimentos feministas há muito que desafiam os sistemas de desigualdade, respondem às crises e criam novas possibilidades para as comunidades marginalizadas e excluídas. A filantropia tem sido fundamental para os avanços rumo a sociedades africanas justas e igualitárias. No entanto, no atual panorama global e continental da filantropia feminista, algumas comunidades e movimentos continuam, em grande parte, invisíveis. 




Os países africanos de língua portuguesa entre os quais se incluem Angola, Cabo Verde, Guiné-Bissau, Moçambique, Guiné Equatorial e São Tomé e Príncipe representam histórias, realidades políticas e contextos sociais diversos. Os seus movimentos feministas são dinâmicos, inovadores e profundamente enraizados nas suas comunidades. Estão a promover a justiça de género em contextos marcados pela privação económica e pela desigualdade, pelas alterações climáticas, por transições democráticas difíceis, pela redução do espaço cívico e pela violência baseada no género.




Apesar deste importante trabalho, estes movimentos continuam a enfrentar obstáculos significativos no acesso a recursos, redes e espaços onde se definem as prioridades feministas de África. O desafio não reside na falta de organização. Trata-se de um ecossistema de financiame

author: Rosebell Kagumire
title: Who Does “Mutual Interest” Serve in an Unequal World? On EU Development Cooperation Pivot
content:
What is mutual interest in an unequal world? That’s what I was reflecting on this week in Brussels, when I joined the “Mutual interests in practice: How should Global Europe balance development, economic and geopolitical objectives?” panel at The Future of EU Development Cooperation, hosted by the European Centre for Development Policy Management (ECDPM) and Oxfam. The discussion came at a decisive moment, as the EU negotiates its next long-term budget and the Global Europe Instrument, while the Commission prepares for consultations with civil society and local authorities from 28 September to 1 October. Regional sessions include “Sub-Saharan Africa”, while global thematic sessions cover human development, the green and digital transition, democracy and human rights, and partnerships.

The EU is pivoting development cooperation towards its own economic, security and foreign policy goals through a “mutual interest” approach. But mutual interest means little unless it confronts the unequal systems that determine whose interests count, whose risks are ignored, and whose lives are rendered negotiable.

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Who Defines Rights in Africa? Transnational Movements and the Unmaking of Human Rights
content:
Globally, hard-won rights and freedoms like sexual and reproductive health and rights, hate speech legislation that protects gender and sexual minorities, gender equality laws and the concept of gender itself, together with other progressive rights, are being challenged and rolled back. Africa, particularly, has become one of the battlegrounds for these contestations led by ultra-conservative groups and organisations identified as 

anti-rights organisations

. These actors are considered ‘anti-rights’ not only because they contest established human rights norms, but also because they hold a different conception of rights rooted in European and religious ideas on tradition, protection and family. This is a regression of rights already hard-fought for in Africa, and it is often clothed in the language of sovereignty, African values and other seemingly neutral terms used to push harmful laws and policies that 

target gender minorities

. These debates are fought at both domestic and international levels, and it is important to see how these actors construct narratives and use mechanisms that were created to enhance human rights protections to target those very rights.
